Motivation
The teams that operate a Kafka cluster have no direct way to see how the clients connected to it are configured. In many organizations, the teams developing and deploying client applications are separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). As a result, an operator investigating a problem has to get the configuration from each application team, which delays the diagnosis and troubleshooting.
The gap matters because client configuration is a common source of problems. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. The gap impact gets more noticeable as Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, so centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical.
This KIP takes the first step in closing this gap by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Each client instance pushes the requested keys once, as soon as it discovers a broker advertising the feature, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows.
At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance or framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. Most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps with one snapshot per client instance, carrying the identifiers needed to group it.
This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework can push one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does it with this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.
The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is collected is a default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name. A change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it, so running clients pick it up at their next restart.
It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications.
This KIP delivers a one-time view of each client instance's configuration.
